name: Lionrapid – AI Translation & Multilingual SEO
author: lionrapid

sections.description:
Take your WordPress site multilingual and reach hundreds of millions of new customers, at a very affordable cost.

Lionrapid translates every page of your site and serves each language as a real page that visitors and search engines read. Install the plugin, click Connect, pick your languages: that’s the whole setup.

Why Lionrapid

  • So easy. Install free from WordPress.org, click Connect to Lionrapid, choose languages on your dashboard. Set up in 5 minutes.
  • Complete multilingual SEO. A URL per language (/fi/, /de/), hreflang with x-default, a canonical per language, the lang attribute, and translated titles, descriptions and social tags. Everything is rendered on the server, so Google, Bing and AI assistants read every language. Works alongside Yoast SEO, Rank Math, AIOSEO and SEOPress.
  • Built for Elementor. Testimonials, counters, tabs, alerts, icon lists and accordions are translated, and your icons stay intact. Gutenberg and the classic editor too.
  • Tested with 80+ of the most popular plugins. WooCommerce, Yoast SEO, Rank Math, Contact Form 7, WPForms, WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, Jetpack, The Events Calendar and many more.
  • Your forms keep working. Contact Form 7, WPForms and Fluent Forms keep every field in every language.
  • Works with your page cache. WP Rocket, W3 Total Cache, WP Super Cache, LiteSpeed Cache, WP Fastest Cache, WP-Optimize, SiteGround Optimizer, Breeze and SpeedyCache are emptied for you when a translation changes.
  • Fast. Pages are translated on your own server, from translations stored in your WordPress database, so a page never waits on us before it is sent, and visitors never see untranslated text flash on the screen.
  • Quality you control. AI translation on models we host, automatic checks on every segment, and review by you or a professional translator before anything goes live. Fix any wording in place with the in-context editor.
  • One memory for everything. Your site, documents and apps share one translation memory and termbase. Export them any time.
  • The best value for money. Plans from €9.90 a month including VAT, with unlimited sites on every plan. A source word counts once against your served-word limit, however many languages you add.

Lionrapid: the choice of winners.

How it works

  1. Install Lionrapid from Plugins → Add New (search “Lionrapid”) and activate it.
  2. Under Settings → Lionrapid, click Connect to Lionrapid and approve it in your Lionrapid account.
  3. Pick your languages on the dashboard. Your site follows at once: a language switcher, translated pages under /fi/, /de/ and so on, and hreflang for search engines.

New and changed text is collected automatically, translated, checked, and goes live when you approve it.

Pricing

The plugin is free and open source (MIT). Translation needs a Lionrapid plan:

  • Basic: €9.90 a month incl. VAT, with 25,000 machine-translation words and 10,000 served words a month.
  • Pro: €24.90 a month, with 100,000 and 50,000.
  • Studio and Business for bigger sites.

Every plan includes unlimited sites, the translation memory and the termbase, and every paid plan starts with a 14-day trial. Cancel anytime. See https://www.lionrapid.com/pricing.

Key features

  • Server-side translation: the page’s HTML is translated before delivery, so search engines see the translated content directly.
  • Formatting kept: inline formatting such as <b> and <a> survives translation.
  • Managed from the dashboard: source and target languages, the switcher and excluded paths come from your Lionrapid project. Changes are pushed to the site immediately, with a 5-minute check as a safety net.
  • Gutenberg blocks: a translation block, a language switcher block and an inline translation editor.
  • Language switcher: three styles (floating, buttons, flags), added to every page automatically or placed where you want it with the block.
  • Language URLs: addresses like /de/, /es/ and /fi/ lead visitors to the right language.
  • SEO: hreflang tags, translated meta descriptions and canonical URLs.
  • New text is collected: text that appears on the live site is sent to your dashboard for translation in the background (wp_cron).

Required external service

This plugin requires a Lionrapid account. It connects to the Lionrapid service at the address shown under Settings → Lionrapid (https://app.lionrapid.com by default).

When activated and configured with a site key, the plugin sends:

  • Translation requests (page content blocks) → server for translation lookup
  • New keys discovered on the live site → server for translation queue
  • Configuration sync requests → server for current project settings

Server endpoints called:

  • GET /api/integrations/config?domain={your-site-domain} — fetches project config
  • GET /api/integrations/translations/{locale}/{namespace} — fetches translations
  • POST /api/integrations/sync/... — pushes newly discovered keys

When your settings hold a publishable key (pk_), your visitors’ browsers also call the Lionrapid service directly, at the API address your Lionrapid project gives (https://app.lionrapid.com by default):

  • to load the translations and language settings for the page they are viewing;
  • to report text on the page that has no translation yet, so it appears in your dashboard.

Like any web request, these calls show the service the visitor’s IP address and browser details. The plugin adds no tracking or analytics. Login and account pages excluded on the dashboard never report text. Without a publishable key, the browser loads translations from your own site instead and calls no Lionrapid address.

The plugin also adds two REST endpoints to your site:

  • POST /wp-json/lionrapid/v1/resync: your Lionrapid dashboard calls it to push configuration changes immediately. It is authenticated with the key stored in your plugin settings.
  • GET /wp-json/lionrapid/v1/api/integrations/translations/{locale}/{namespace}: public and read-only. It serves your site’s translations to the visitor’s browser, so the browser never needs a key.

Lionrapid’s terms of service: https://www.lionrapid.com/terms. Privacy policy: https://www.lionrapid.com/privacy.

Without a site key

Until you enter a site key, the plugin calls no external service. It does start preparing your pages for translation as soon as it is active (language links and markers in the HTML), so activate it once your Lionrapid account is ready.
sections.installation:
1. In Plugins → Add New Plugin, search for “Lionrapid”, then click Install Now on Lionrapid – AI Translation & Multilingual SEO and Activate. (You can also upload lionrapid-translation-<version>.zip from https://github.com/LionRapid/lionrapid-wordpress/releases under Upload Plugin; it installs as the same plugin.)
  2. Visit Settings → Lionrapid and click Connect to Lionrapid.
  3. Approve the code in your Lionrapid account, then click Confirm on the settings page. Instead of connecting, you can paste the site key from the WordPress tab of your Lionrapid dashboard (a publishable key starting with pk_) and click Save key. Sites configured earlier with a master key (sk_) keep working unchanged.
  4. The plugin pulls your project settings (languages, switcher, excluded paths) from the dashboard automatically.
  5. Language URLs like /de/ are set up automatically when your languages change. If one answers “not found”, click Refresh language URLs on the same page.
sections.faq:
Is the plugin free?

Yes. The plugin is free and open source on WordPress.org. Translation plans start at €9.90 a month including VAT, for unlimited sites, and every paid plan starts with a 14-day trial you can cancel anytime.

Is it good for multilingual SEO?

Yes, it’s complete. Every language gets its own URL, hreflang with x-default, a canonical, and translated titles, descriptions and social tags. Pages are rendered on the server, so search engines and AI assistants read the translation. Your SEO plugin (Yoast SEO, Rank Math, AIOSEO, SEOPress) keeps working in every language.

Does it work with Elementor?

Yes. Elementor’s free widgets are translated, including the text Elementor places outside paragraphs (testimonials, counters, alerts, tab titles), and their icons stay in place. The one exception is Text Path, which draws its letters with a script.

Does it work with WooCommerce, forms and caching plugins?

Yes. Lionrapid is tested with 80+ of the most popular plugins, WooCommerce among them. Contact Form 7, WPForms and Fluent Forms keep every field in every language, and nine popular cache plugins are emptied automatically when a translation changes. Path rules on the dashboard keep /cart/, /checkout/ and similar pages untranslated if you prefer.

How fast is the setup?

About five minutes: install, click Connect to Lionrapid, pick your languages.

Can I check translations before they go live?

Yes. Nothing goes live until you or your translator approve it. Edit any wording right on the page with the in-context editor.

How many sites and languages can I have?

Unlimited sites on every plan. A source word counts once against your served-word limit, however many languages you serve.

Do I need a Lionrapid account?

Yes. Sign up at https://www.lionrapid.com, then click Connect to Lionrapid under Settings → Lionrapid and approve the site in your account.

Can I use it without server-side translation?

Yes. In the Lionrapid dashboard, turn off “Server-side translate initial page render” for your project. The plugin will then rely on JavaScript-side translation only, applied via MutationObserver after page load.

How does it handle new strings that haven’t been translated yet?

The plugin scans the block-level strings of every page it renders, in your source language too. On a translated page, each string is looked up in the cached translations. A string Lionrapid does not know yet is queued for sync via wp_cron, so a visit to a page in your source language is enough to send its new strings. They appear in the Lionrapid editor for human or machine translation, and the next page load gets the translated version.

Does it work with my theme or page builder?

The plugin translates the finished page, whichever theme or builder made it. Path rules let you exclude /cart/, /checkout/, /wp-admin/, and similar paths from translation if needed (configured on the dashboard).

Is my API key visible to visitors?

The key the plugin prints for the browser is a publishable key (pk_), which is designed to be public — it can read your translations and register new strings for translation, nothing else. The plugin refuses to print anything that is not a pk_ key: if your settings hold a master key (sk_), it stays server-side and the browser is pointed at this site’s own read-only translation endpoint instead. A master key is never written into your page HTML.

Where are my settings stored?

In wp_options under the key lionrapid_settings. Your site key, the service address and the on/off switch are set in Settings → Lionrapid. Everything else (languages, namespace, switcher, exclude paths) is read-only and overwritten by the dashboard sync.

How do I uninstall cleanly?

Deactivating the plugin stops it and keeps your settings. Deleting it from Plugins removes its settings, saved translations and scheduled jobs (on a multisite network, on every site).

I installed an earlier version from a ZIP file. How do I switch to the directory version?

ZIP files before 1.3.1 installed into the folder lionrapid; the directory version installs into lionrapid-translation. WordPress treats them as two plugins, but they share one set of settings.

Install Lionrapid from the directory and activate it. If the old copy is still active, the new one deactivates it and takes over with your site key and settings. Then delete the old copy from Plugins; your settings stay. The Plugins screen and Settings → Lionrapid point out the old copy while it is still installed.

Before 1.4.2, deleting the old copy removed the shared settings. If you installed an earlier version from the directory and still have the old copy, update to 1.4.2 first, then delete it.

ZIP files from 1.3.1 on install into lionrapid-translation, the directory’s own folder, so WordPress treats a ZIP install and a directory install as the same plugin: updates from the directory arrive in Dashboard → Updates either way, and your settings are kept.

Where is the source code of the bundled JavaScript?

The plugin’s own minified scripts in assets/dist/ are built from the TypeScript sources that ship in assets/src/.

The three scripts in assets/dist/js/vendor/ come from the open-source Lionrapid SDK, https://github.com/LionRapid/lionrapid-sdk (MIT, packages/core, built by packages/core/build.browser.js):

  • lionrapid.auto.min.js: the language switcher and in-page translation, from src/browser/index.ts. Its unminified build ships beside it as lionrapid.auto.dev.js.
  • lionrapid.iife.min.js: the library the Gutenberg blocks use in the editor, from src/index.ts.
  • lionrapid.editor.min.js: the visual translation editor, loaded only during an editor session, from src/browser/editor/editor-init.ts.
sections.changelog:
1.5.1

  • Changed: the plugin is now called “Lionrapid – AI Translation & Multilingual SEO”, and
    its directory page describes it anew: what it does for your site, how to set it up with
    Connect to Lionrapid, the plans and a buyer’s FAQ. No code changes; your settings and
    translations stay as they are.

1.5.0

  • New: text that page builders such as Elementor put straight into a div or span is
    translated: testimonials, counters, tab titles, alerts and similar widgets. Inline SVG
    icons stay intact.
  • New: dropdown options, a form’s legend (WPForms, Fluent Forms) and bold or emphasised
    text standing on its own are translated.
  • New: after a translation change, the page cache is cleared on WP Fastest Cache,
    WP-Optimize, SiteGround Optimizer, Breeze and SpeedyCache too, as it already was on
    WP Rocket, W3 Total Cache, WP Super Cache and LiteSpeed Cache.
  • Changed: a line that contains a link is now translated as one text (“Proudly powered by
    WordPress”), where only the link was translated before. On a site that is already
    translated, such lines show the original text until their new translation is approved.
  • Changed: text without letters, such as a price, » or ×, is no longer sent for
    translation.
  • Changed: text marked notranslate or translate="no", and icon-font words such as
    Material Icons, keep their original text. So do the language names in the
    [lionrapid_switcher] dropdown.
  • Fixed: form fields inside a translated label or paragraph, such as Contact Form 7’s
    inputs, and embedded iframes no longer disappear from translated pages.
  • Fixed: a coming-soon or maintenance page that a plugin prints early (UnderConstructionPage)
    is translated.
  • Fixed: a post type archive under a language prefix, such as /fi/events/ from The Events
    Calendar, no longer returns 404.
  • Fixed: comments, footers and other sections inside a translated text are translated
    (the Latest Comments block).
  • Fixed: titles, alt texts and placeholders are translated on elements that also carry
    Alpine, Vue or underscore attributes (Variation Swatches).
  • Fixed: icons keep their shapes and colours on translated pages, and an icon with a title
    no longer hides the text of its button or link.
  • Fixed: single-quoted attributes, such as Elementor’s classes, are no longer lost on
    translated pages.
  • Fixed: og:url on a translated page points at the translated page, and hreflang and
    canonical links keep a non-standard port.

1.4.2

  • Fixed: activating Lionrapid Translation while an older copy installed from a ZIP
    (in plugins/lionrapid/) is still active no longer fails with a fatal error. The new
    copy takes over and deactivates the old one; your connection and settings carry over.
  • Fixed: deleting that older copy no longer deletes your settings. Its uninstall used to
    remove the settings the two copies share, which disconnected the site.
  • New: the Plugins screen and Settings → Lionrapid say when an older copy is still
    installed, and that it can be deleted.

1.4.1

  • Changed: the plugin now requires PHP 8.1. On PHP 8.0 it could not be activated.
  • Changed: activation no longer switches Plain permalinks to /%postname%/ by itself.
    Settings → Lionrapid says when your permalinks need changing for language addresses.
  • Changed: the page-cache notice shows only on Settings → Lionrapid, not on every
    admin screen.
  • Fixed: settings saved through the settings form or synced from your dashboard are
    cleaned field by field; invalid language codes are dropped.
  • Fixed: the plugin reads WordPress’s own addresses (REST, admin, login) instead of
    assuming the default ones, so a custom REST prefix works.
  • Fixed: the translation-editor block no longer contacts Lionrapid before the site is
    connected, and dashboard pushes are limited to one run a minute.
  • Fixed: no missing-file notices or 404s for block scripts in the block editor.

1.4.0

  • New: a simpler settings page. Connection, Translation and Languages each sit on one
    card, the status shows at the top (Connected, Waiting for approval, Not connected), and
    the connection code is shown large with a Copy button. Explanations moved into small ⓘ
    labels that open on hover, keyboard focus or tap. Technical details are under Advanced.
  • Fixed: “Connect to Lionrapid” always starts on the first click, also before the page’s
    script has loaded.
  • Fixed: a top-corner language switcher no longer covers your theme’s header menu.
  • Fixed: a visitor’s browser no longer shows a stored copy of translations from another
    Lionrapid project on the same site, and a removed translation stops being shown.
  • The page language (<html lang>) follows the language the visitor picks.

1.3.2

  • Fixed: the first Save on the settings page, and Sync Now, could drop the languages,
    namespace and switcher settings arriving from your dashboard, while still showing a
    successful Last sync. They came back only at the next background sync.
  • Fixed: with “Enable Plugin” or “Emit hreflang tags” turned off, Sync Now could turn
    them back on.
  • A sync whose settings could not be saved now reports an error instead of success.
  • The FAQ now says that pages in your source language are scanned too: that is how new
    strings reach Lionrapid.
  • The redirect to a visitor’s language uses wp_safe_redirect(), which only follows
    addresses on your own site.

1.3.1

  • Now in the WordPress plugin directory as “Lionrapid Translation”. The text domain is
    lionrapid-translation, the directory’s name for the plugin, so translations of the
    settings screen can come from translate.wordpress.org.
  • The readable TypeScript sources of the bundled scripts ship with the plugin, in
    assets/src/.
  • The readme describes the plugin as it is today: three switcher styles, the current
    button names, what deleting the plugin removes, the service it connects to, and
    what visitors’ browsers send to it when you use a publishable key.
  • The plugin folder is now lionrapid-translation, the same as the directory
    install, so a ZIP install and a directory install are one plugin. ZIP files
    before 1.3.1 installed into lionrapid; see the FAQ before switching.
  • Deleting the plugin keeps your settings while another copy of it is still
    installed.
  • The translation cache rows carry the plugin’s lionrapid_ prefix. The old rows
    are removed once after updating and your translations are fetched again on the
    next page view.
  • The same-origin translation endpoint moved into the plugin’s own namespace:
    /wp-json/lionrapid/v1/api/integrations/translations/{locale}/{namespace}. The
    old /wp-json/api/integrations/... address is gone. A page your host cached
    before updating may ask the old address until that cache expires; its
    server-side translation is unaffected.
  • Every value read from the request is unslashed and sanitized, with web addresses
    kept intact, and each admin action checks its security token itself.

1.3.0

  • The settings page now speaks plainly. Labels and messages were written for the
    developers who built the plugin, not for the people who install it — so a failure
    said things like “Invalid response format” and left you nowhere to go. Every
    message now says what happened and what to do about it.

  • The server address defaults to the real one. A fresh install pointed at localhost,
    an address that only exists on a developer’s own machine, so the first connection
    test could never succeed. Sites already set up are unaffected — your saved address
    is kept.

  • Every button shows its own progress and result. Test connection, Sync now, Clear
    cache and Update language URLs now behave the same way: the button tells you it is
    working, then whether it worked, and the answer stays on screen underneath instead
    of vanishing.

  • When something fails you get a plain explanation and a next step, with the
    technical detail behind a “Details” link for when support needs it.

1.2.6

  • Fix: visitors whose browser is set to another language now reach that language
    from your home page, even when the page is served from your host’s cache.
    Previously the redirect ran in PHP, and on a cached page PHP never runs — so a
    Finnish visitor landing on a warm home page simply saw English. The choice is
    now made in the browser, which still runs when the cache is serving.
    Your home page stays cached for everyone; only the language decision moved.

1.2.5

  • Fix: a translation you removed or unapproved could keep appearing on your site
    forever. Each string was stored twice — once on its own and once inside a
    bundle — and refreshing replaced the bundle without ever clearing the individual
    copy, which is the one the plugin reads first.
  • Fix: choosing your own language now sticks. Picking the site’s main language
    from the switcher could be overridden by your browser’s language on the next
    visit, sending you back to the language you had just left.
  • Fix: language-prefixed URLs like /fi/about/ now resolve the same way /about/
    does, including nested pages and content from other plugins. Cache and SEO tools
    that ask WordPress “which page is this URL?” previously got no answer for a
    translated page.
  • Fix: “Clear Translations” also clears the bookkeeping that tracks how fresh your
    translations are.
  • Fix: deactivating the plugin now stops all three of its scheduled jobs, not one.
  • New: on hosts with a page cache the plugin can clear — WP Rocket, W3TC,
    LiteSpeed, WP Super Cache — it clears it automatically when translations change.
  • New: on WordPress.com, where plugins cannot clear the cache, you get a notice in
    the admin when your visitors are being served old pages, and how to clear it. It
    appears only when translations actually change, and once dismissed it stays
    dismissed until they change again.
  • New: on WordPress.com your language choice is now part of the page-cache key, so
    a visitor who prefers Finnish is no longer served the page cached for an English
    visitor.

1.2.4

  • Fix: “Clear Translations” now really clears them on hosts that keep a
    persistent object cache, WordPress.com among them. The rows were being
    deleted, but a cached copy was still served, so old translations came back
    and no amount of clearing helped. The same stale copies also made every
    string look like one the site had already reported, so the site quietly
    stopped sending new content to your dashboard. If your site is on such a
    host, press Clear Translations once after updating.
  • Fix: the plugin’s own short-lived caches are cleared too. On a site with a
    persistent object cache those are not kept in the database at all, so the
    previous cleanup silently matched nothing.
  • Change: a resync from the dashboard now refreshes translations as well as
    settings, so an edit reaches your site without waiting for the next
    scheduled check.

1.2.3

  • Fix: translation changes now appear on the FIRST page load. The refresh ran
    after the page had already been sent, so a page always showed the previous
    version and a reload was needed to see an edit.
  • Fix: saving a new API key no longer silently reverts to the old one. The
    settings page reported success while the previous key was written back.
  • Fix: the server URL you configure is the one the plugin calls. A legacy
    setting could override it invisibly, so requests went to the old host and
    failed with an error blaming the API key.
  • Fix: the dashboard’s minimum-text-length setting now reaches the site. It was
    declared and honoured everywhere except the one place that reads it from the
    server, so sites stayed on the built-in default.

1.2.2

  • Fix: “Clear Translations” now actually clears them. It was deleting from a
    cache layer the plugin never wrote to, and reported success because the delete
    matched zero rows rather than failing.
  • Fix: the source-language home page is reachable again. A visitor arriving at
    your site with no referer — a typed address, a bookmark, a search result — was
    redirected to their guessed language every time, with no way back to /. An
    inferred language now redirects once; an explicit choice from the switcher
    still always applies.

1.2.1

  • Fix: og: and twitter: social preview text is now translated. A shared link
    showed the source language even on a translated page, because the preview
    meta tags were never extracted for translation.
  • Housekeeping: removed translationMode, a setting nothing ever read.

1.2.0

  • Feature: regional locale routing (for example /pt-br/), with BCP-47 hreflang
    and Accept-Language quality-value parsing.
  • Feature: SEO plugin coexistence — Yoast and similar plugins are detected, and
    canonical/hreflang output defers to them instead of emitting a second,
    conflicting set.
  • Feature: localized sitemap alternates for Yoast.
  • Feature: honours the noindex-locales setting, so a locale still under review
    is not indexed before it is ready.
  • Change: the plugin authenticates with a publishable (pk_) key, and prefers
    the API host the server advertises over a hardcoded one.

1.1.2

  • Fix: background sync no longer retries in a loop when the API key is missing
    or the server answers 4xx.
  • Fix: no If-None-Match header while the translations cache is empty — the
    request could return 304 with nothing to render from.
  • Fix: exact attribute-name matching when detecting no-translate markers, so a
    name that merely starts the same is no longer treated as a match.
  • Fix: the fallback class loader mirrors src/ again, so a fresh install cannot
    fatal on a class the loader never required.

1.1.1

  • Security: hex-escape the inline config script so a config value cannot break
    out of the <script> tag (including the <!--<script> mXSS vector).
  • Fix: editor-pushed formatted translations now store under the real
    translation key instead of a numeric style index.
  • Build: the release now fails if the readme Stable tag and plugin header
    Version drift apart, so wp.org always ships the built version.

1.1.0

  • Feature: attribute translation — alt, title, placeholder, meta and input
    values.
  • Feature: href and canonical rewriting on localized paths.
  • Feature: auth-page contract — configured paths never sync keys (GDPR).
  • Fix: the same-site referer guard never fired, because a bare host was
    compared against one carrying a port.
  • Fix: /{lang}/ home now resolves in the request filter, rewrite rules flush on
    a language change, and the locale redirect is skipped during editor sessions.
  • Fix: decode HTML entities in the markup parser, so PHP and JavaScript derive
    the same translation key for the same text.

1.0.1

  • Fix: translated Pages (not just Posts) now resolve at /{lang}/ URLs.
  • Fix: editor URLs like /es/?__lr_editor= no longer 404 (query string was
    being captured as the post slug).
  • Add: pretty permalinks are enabled automatically on activation when the
    site is on the default plain structure (a custom structure is left
    untouched), so /{lang}/ routing works out of the box.
  • Fix: config-sync cron is scheduled on init, silencing a WP 6.7
    “textdomain loaded too early” notice.

1.0.0

Initial public release.

  • Server-side block-level translation via output buffering.
  • Dashboard-managed config sync: languages, namespace, switcher, exclude paths, output-buffering toggle pulled from the LionRapid server.
  • Real-time config push via POST /wp-json/lionrapid/v1/resync from the dashboard.
  • 5-minute wp_cron fallback for config sync.
  • Gutenberg blocks: translation, language switcher, translation editor.
  • Language switcher auto-inject with four styles.
  • URL prefix routing for non-source languages.
  • SEO hreflang + translated meta descriptions.
  • Background sync of newly discovered keys via wp_cron.

How it works

  1. Install Lionrapid from Plugins → Add New (search “Lionrapid”) and activate it.
  2. Under Settings → Lionrapid, click Connect to Lionrapid and approve it in your Lionrapid account.
  3. Pick your languages on the dashboard. Your site follows at once: a language switcher, translated pages under /fi/, /de/ and so on, and hreflang for search engines.

New and changed text is collected automatically, translated, checked, and goes live when you approve it.

Pricing

The plugin is free and open source (MIT). Translation needs a Lionrapid plan:

  • Basic: €9.90 a month incl. VAT, with 25,000 machine-translation words and 10,000 served words a month.
  • Pro: €24.90 a month, with 100,000 and 50,000.
  • Studio and Business for bigger sites.

Every plan includes unlimited sites, the translation memory and the termbase, and every paid plan starts with a 14-day trial. Cancel anytime. See https://www.lionrapid.com/pricing.

Key features

  • Server-side translation: the page’s HTML is translated before delivery, so search engines see the translated content directly.
  • Formatting kept: inline formatting such as <b> and <a> survives translation.
  • Managed from the dashboard: source and target languages, the switcher and excluded paths come from your Lionrapid project. Changes are pushed to the site immediately, with a 5-minute check as a safety net.
  • Gutenberg blocks: a translation block, a language switcher block and an inline translation editor.
  • Language switcher: three styles (floating, buttons, flags), added to every page automatically or placed where you want it with the block.
  • Language URLs: addresses like /de/, /es/ and /fi/ lead visitors to the right language.
  • SEO: hreflang tags, translated meta descriptions and canonical URLs.
  • New text is collected: text that appears on the live site is sent to your dashboard for translation in the background (wp_cron).

Required external service

This plugin requires a Lionrapid account. It connects to the Lionrapid service at the address shown under Settings → Lionrapid (https://app.lionrapid.com by default).

When activated and configured with a site key, the plugin sends:

  • Translation requests (page content blocks) → server for translation lookup
  • New keys discovered on the live site → server for translation queue
  • Configuration sync requests → server for current project settings

Server endpoints called:

  • GET /api/integrations/config?domain={your-site-domain} — fetches project config
  • GET /api/integrations/translations/{locale}/{namespace} — fetches translations
  • POST /api/integrations/sync/... — pushes newly discovered keys

When your settings hold a publishable key (pk_), your visitors’ browsers also call the Lionrapid service directly, at the API address your Lionrapid project gives (https://app.lionrapid.com by default):

  • to load the translations and language settings for the page they are viewing;
  • to report text on the page that has no translation yet, so it appears in your dashboard.

Like any web request, these calls show the service the visitor’s IP address and browser details. The plugin adds no tracking or analytics. Login and account pages excluded on the dashboard never report text. Without a publishable key, the browser loads translations from your own site instead and calls no Lionrapid address.

The plugin also adds two REST endpoints to your site:

  • POST /wp-json/lionrapid/v1/resync: your Lionrapid dashboard calls it to push configuration changes immediately. It is authenticated with the key stored in your plugin settings.
  • GET /wp-json/lionrapid/v1/api/integrations/translations/{locale}/{namespace}: public and read-only. It serves your site’s translations to the visitor’s browser, so the browser never needs a key.

Lionrapid’s terms of service: https://www.lionrapid.com/terms. Privacy policy: https://www.lionrapid.com/privacy.

Without a site key

Until you enter a site key, the plugin calls no external service. It does start preparing your pages for translation as soon as it is active (language links and markers in the HTML), so activate it once your Lionrapid account is ready.
